awd_titl_txt: Conference: 2025 Lactic Acid Bacteria Biology, Symbioses and Applications GRC
awd_abstract_narration:
The Gordon Research Conference on Lactic Acid Bacteria Biology, Symbioses, and Applications will bring together researchers to explore the beneficial roles of lactic acid bacteria in health, food systems, and the environment. This meeting will unite scientists from fields as diverse as microbiology, nutrition, medicine, and synthetic biology. Lactic acid bacteria are essential for making many fermented foods and are associated with health benefits, but much remains unknown about how they function. The conference will create a unique environment where scientists at all career stages, from students to senior leaders, can share new, unpublished findings and foster collaborations. A companion Gordon Research Seminar, organized by early-career researchers, will emphasize peer networking and professional development. By encouraging the exchange of ideas across disciplines and generations, the meeting will spark new discoveries with the potential to improve human health, advance food innovation and the bioeconomy, and strengthen scientific training. 

The Gordon Research Conference will focus on advancing mechanistic understanding of lactic acid bacteria across varied environments from fermented foods to the animal gut, with an emphasis on cross-disciplinary challenges in microbial genetics, host adaptation, metabolism, and therapeutic development. Specific research areas include the molecular basis of lactic acid bacteria-host interactions, metabolic cross-feeding within microbial communities, bacterial adaptation to different environments, and the development of lactic acid bacteria-based therapeutic delivery systems. The program will feature nine thematic sessions ranging from phage-bacteria dynamics to symbioses in the human gut and vagina. Experimental approaches discussed will include functional genomics, synthetic biology, live microbial imaging, and systems biology analyses. The conference aims to catalyze new collaborations and technical innovations that will push the frontiers of microbiome science, fermentation biology, and microbial therapeutics.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The 2025 Lactic Acid Bacteria Biology, Symbioses and Applications Gordon Research Conference (GRC), held July 13-18 in Ventura, California, brought together 103 scientists from universities, industry, and research organizations. Participants came from North America, Europe, and Asia and represented career stages ranging from graduate students to senior faculty and research leaders. An associated Gordon Research Seminar (GRS), held July 12-13 for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, enrolled 41 participants; 40 continued into the main conference.

Lactic acid bacteria are best known for their roles in fermented foods such as yogurt and sourdough bread, but they are also important members of human, animal, and insect microbiomes and are increasingly used in medicine and biotechnology. The meeting presented new, largely unpublished research on how these bacteria live and evolve in different environments; interact with hosts and other microbes; influence health and disease; respond to viruses that infect bacteria; and can be developed as therapeutics. Sessions addressed bacteria in environmental settings, the gastrointestinal and vaginal microbiomes, non-mammalian hosts, microbial products, bacteriophages, and applications relevant to food security, human health, and the environment.

Scientific talks were deliberately paired with substantial discussion time, while four poster sessions, shared meals, and informal afternoon interactions encouraged exchange across disciplines and career levels. This structure allowed participants to compare methods, identify common questions, and form relationships that can support future research collaborations.

The GRS provided additional leadership and communication training for early-career scientists. Trainees presented research on microbial interactions, ecological niches, evolution, and adaptation, and served as speakers, discussion leaders, and organizers. Experienced mentors and trainee moderators promoted active participation so that attendees were contributors rather than spectators.

NSF funding expanded access by supporting 10 participants at the main conference and 9 at the seminar. Across these awards, support reached 11 graduate students, seven postdoctoral researchers, and one assistant professor. Awardees contributed as speakers, discussion leaders, a poster presenter, and a seminar organizer, directly strengthening the scientific program and early-career visibility.

Participant feedback was extremely positive. Attendees described cutting-edge scientific content, strong networking between junior and senior scientists, a respectful and collegial environment, a diverse and engaging speaker pool, and interactive poster sessions. Overall, the project advanced knowledge of beneficial microbes while strengthening an international community working on challenges in human health, food production, and the environment.
